summary: Gives guidance and recommendations to developers building X.509 certification paths in applications. Following it should help applications build valid paths across a wide range of PKI environments. It is informational.

eli5.summary: To trust a stranger, you ask who vouches for them, and who vouches for that person, until you reach someone you know. This memo gives tips for finding that chain of vouching.

subtitle: How to find the chain of certificates linking a public key to a trusted authority.

tldr.problem: When an application receives a digital certificate, it needs to verify that the public key in it is genuine. Before validating the certificate, it must first find the chain of intermediate certificates that connect it back to a trusted root authority, but there are many possible paths depending on the PKI structure.
tldr.mechanism: Path-building algorithms search for the shortest valid chain by either starting from the target certificate and working back to a trust anchor, or starting from the trust anchor and working toward the target. Optimizations help the algorithm try the most promising branches first rather than exhaustively searching all possibilities.
tldr.outcome: Applications can reliably discover valid certification paths in any PKI structure, including complex mesh and bridge PKIs with multiple trust anchors. This enables broad PKI interoperability.

facts.label: Path building directions
facts.value: 2: forward (from target) and reverse (from trust anchor)

facts.label: Recommended algorithm
facts.value: Depth-first tree traversal with optimization scoring

today: RFC 4158 is an Informational RFC from 2005 and has not been obsoleted. As PKI systems continue to grow in complexity, with growing use of cross-certification and bridge PKIs, this guidance on path building remains relevant to developers building certificate-enabled applications.

sections.title: The Certificate Chain Problem
sections.content:
When an application needs to verify a digital signature or establish secure communication, it uses the public key stored in an X.509 certificate. But before trusting that key, the application must verify that the certificate itself is genuine. It does this by checking that the certificate's signature was created by the certificate's issuer, which is another CA (Certification Authority).

The application does not directly trust the issuing CA either, so it must find the certificate that the issuing CA received from its superior. This process continues up the chain until reaching a trust anchor, an authority whose public key the application has been configured to trust (such as a root CA certificate pre-installed in a browser).

This ordered chain of certificates is called a certification path. Finding this path before validation is the job of certification path building. Unlike path validation, which is standardized, path building is not because the method of finding the path does not affect whether it is valid. However, the ability to find valid paths is crucial, and different PKI structures create different challenges.
sections.eli5: You receive a certificate claiming to be from a bank. You look for a chain showing that the certificate came from a trusted authority, one certificate at a time, until you reach the root authority you already trust.

sections.title: Four Common PKI Structures and Their Path-Finding Challenges
sections.content:
The RFC describes four common ways that Certification Authorities are organized:

Hierarchical PKI: A single root CA (or a small list of roots) at the top certifies intermediate CAs, which in turn certify end-user certificates. Finding a path is simple: start with the target certificate and walk up the chain until reaching the root. Most widely-deployed systems use this structure.

Mesh PKI: Multiple CAs act as peers, each certifying others in a web of interconnections. There may be many possible paths from the target to any given trust anchor. Worse, in a fully-meshed network of n CAs, there can be millions of different paths between two points, making exhaustive search infeasible.

Bridge PKI: A single bridge certification authority (BCA) sits between multiple hierarchical PKIs, cross-certifying with exactly one CA in each PKI. This scales better than a mesh (relationships grow linearly instead of exponentially) but creates more complex path-building requirements because applications must handle the structures of all the PKIs being bridged.

Hybrid PKI: A combination of the above, such as a hierarchical PKI that cross-certifies with a mesh PKI. Path building must handle all the complexities of both structures.
sections.eli5: A hierarchy is a family tree. A mesh is everyone friends with everyone. A bridge is a single hub that connects multiple groups. A hybrid is a mix.

sections.title: Forward and Reverse Path Building
sections.content:
A certification path-building algorithm can search in two directions:

Forward direction: Start with the target certificate (the one being verified) and search for its issuer, then the issuer's issuer, and so on, until reaching a trust anchor. This approach works well when many trust anchors exist or when issuing-authority information is readily available (for example, stored in the certificate itself via the authorityInformationAccess extension).

Reverse direction: Start with a trust anchor and search for certificates it has issued, then certificates issued by those CAs, and so on, until finding a path to the target certificate. This approach works better when there is only one trust anchor or when reverse cross-certification information is readily available in a directory.

The RFC explains that both directions can be viewed as traversing a tree, regardless of PKI complexity. The key insight is that certificates cannot repeat in a path (per X.509 rules), which prevents infinite loops. However, the RFC recommends further restricting paths to avoid repeating the same subject name and public key pair, even in different certificates, as this eliminates convoluted, unintended paths while keeping all necessary paths available.
sections.eli5: You can start at the certificate and climb up to the root, or start at the root and climb down to the certificate. Both should find the same path if it exists.

sections.title: Optimizing the Search: Finding the Best Path First
sections.content:
A naive path-building algorithm that tries every possible path can be extremely slow. In a mesh PKI with many interconnections, a simple depth-first search might traverse millions of candidate paths. The RFC recommends an optimization-based approach: assign priority scores to candidate certificates so that the algorithm tries the most promising branches first.

The RFC suggests many scoring criteria, including: whether a certificate has the basicConstraints extension marking it as a CA certificate, whether the signature algorithm is recognized by the application, whether the certificate validity period includes the current time, whether the certificate has been previously validated, whether the issuer DN matches what the algorithm expects, whether the certificate appears to come from a local cache, and whether certificate policy constraints are satisfied.

With these optimizations, the algorithm builds valid paths efficiently in most cases. The authors recommend a depth-first tree traversal with proper sorting at each decision point, rather than a breadth-first search or an exhaustive graph search.

The RFC also addresses specific challenges such as distinguishing between true loops (which violate X.509) and valid uses of the same CA in different parts of a bridge PKI, detecting dead ends early, and handling different distinguished name encodings that may look different but represent the same entity.
sections.eli5: Rather than checking every possible path, the algorithm is smart about which ones to try first. It marks certificates that are more likely to work and tries those first, skipping less promising options.

sections.title: Certificate Retrieval and Path Validation
sections.content:
Certification path building requires retrieving certificates from various sources: LDAP directories, HTTP URLs, Authority Information Access (AIA) extensions in certificates, CRL distribution points, or data provided directly by the application protocol (such as an email message with attached certificates).

The RFC discusses caching strategies to improve retrieval performance, parallel fetching to reduce latency, and how to properly order retrieval attempts to find needed certificates quickly. It also mentions special considerations for building certification paths for revocation signer certificates, which are certificates used to sign Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) or OCSP responses. These may require separate path-building logic because they may be issued by different CAs than the certificates whose revocation they attest to.

Finally, the RFC covers security considerations: applications must guard against attacks where path-building logic is tricked into accepting invalid paths, must properly handle policy constraints and name constraints, and should be aware that path building across multiple PKI domains introduces additional trust assumptions.
sections.eli5: Once the algorithm knows what certificates to look for, it has to actually find them. They might be in a local cache, on a server somewhere, or attached to the certificate itself. The memo explains how to fetch them efficiently and safely.
